title: The Punisher
edition: Mark Goldblatt feature starring Dolph Lundgren; standard R-rated home-video release, excluding the extended workprint.
synopsis: When gangsters’ children are kidnapped, Frank Castle gets most of them to safety. Reaching the last boy means working alongside his father, a man Castle has every reason to distrust.
verdictRationale: Castle sees that children have no share in their parents’ guilt. He even risks arrest to get them away. Yet the film repeatedly gives his private campaign of killing the force of justice. Its sharpest challenge to that pattern comes from Tommy, who has just lost his father and lets Castle live.
ageRationale: Armed adults use children as hostages. A boy faces the man who has killed his father. These scenes of bereavement and intimidation accompany repeated lethal violence.
reflection: What kind of future is left to Tommy when the adults around him model revenge? Castle’s parting advice would carry more weight if Tommy could see him live by it. The boy’s hesitation gives an Orthodox family an opening to discuss mercy toward a person who has caused real harm.

title: Man-Thing
edition: Brett Leonard’s 96-minute Lionsgate home/streaming feature with Matthew Le Nevez; advisories refer to the adult-rated version.
synopsis: In Bywater, a new sheriff investigates disappearances near an oil operation. What looks like a search for a suspect becomes an inquiry into who owned the land and what happened to its former custodian.
verdictRationale: Williams gradually tests Schist’s accusations against the bodies and testimony. That willingness to revise a judgment is admirable. Schist’s confession exposes the cost of treating a community’s land as his possession. Graphic deaths and a vengeful guardian supply much of the horror, leaving little room for restitution.
ageRationale: The opening includes sex and nudity in a canoe. Later, the investigation repeatedly brings the viewer close to mutilated remains, including a disturbing discovery during an autopsy.
reflection: A sheriff can listen to a landowner and still owe the accused a hearing. Consider how readily a powerful person’s account can become the town’s accepted story. The swamp guardian belongs to this film’s supernatural fiction; the duty to hear a neighbor fairly applies in ordinary life.
